text: A platform team is rolling out Claude Code to a 40-engineer organization. Different squads work on separate repositories with different compliance requirements, and the team wants consistent tool permissions, shared custom slash commands, and standardized MCP server access without engineers manually reconfiguring settings on each machine. Which approach best achieves this at scale?
options: Ask each engineer to individually install and configure Claude Code with their own preferred settings to maximize flexibility
Grant every engineer full administrative access to all MCP servers and tools so no one is ever blocked by missing permissions

Define and version-control project-level configuration files (permissions, custom commands, MCP server allowlists) that are checked into each repository so settings are consistent and auditable across the team
Disable all custom commands and MCP integrations organization-wide to eliminate configuration drift
correct_answer: Define and version-control project-level configuration files (permissions, custom commands, MCP server allowlists) that are checked into each repository so settings are consistent and auditable across the team
explanation: Configuring Claude Code for teams at scale requires reproducible, version-controlled configuration rather than ad hoc per-engineer setup. Checking in project-level config (permissions, custom commands, allowed MCP servers, option C) ensures consistency across repositories, supports compliance requirements that vary by squad, and makes changes auditable through normal code review. Letting each engineer configure independently (A) creates drift and compliance risk. Granting blanket admin access (B) violates least-privilege principles central to secure tool configuration. Disabling integrations entirely (D) eliminates productivity gains the tooling is meant to provide.

text: A development team wants to use AI-assisted tooling to reduce the time engineers spend on repetitive code review comments (style violations, missing tests, obvious null-pointer risks) so senior reviewers can focus on architecture and business logic. Which workflow change best improves developer productivity while preserving review quality?
options: Integrate a Claude-based review step into the CI pipeline that flags style issues, missing test coverage, and common defect patterns as PR comments, leaving final merge approval to human reviewers
Replace human code review entirely with an automated Claude-based approval step that merges pull requests without any human sign-off
Require engineers to manually copy each file into a chat interface and paste back suggestions before opening a pull request
Disable automated linting and testing tools so Claude is the sole source of code quality feedback
correct_answer: Integrate a Claude-based review step into the CI pipeline that flags style issues, missing test coverage, and common defect patterns as PR comments, leaving final merge approval to human reviewers
explanation: Improving developer workflows with AI-assisted tooling means embedding automation where it removes repetitive burden while preserving human judgment for higher-stakes decisions. Integrating an automated review step into CI (A) frees senior reviewers to focus on architecture and logic while keeping merge authority with humans. Fully automating approvals (B) removes necessary human oversight and risks quality regressions. Manual copy-paste workflows (C) do not improve productivity since they add friction. Removing existing tooling (D) discards complementary, deterministic checks that AI review should augment, not replace.

text: An on-call engineer is paged for a production incident: a Claude-powered service is returning elevated error rates. The engineer wants to use Claude Code to accelerate root-cause triage. Which use of the tool is most appropriate for supporting debugging and operational issue resolution during the incident?
options: Ask Claude Code to automatically deploy a rollback to the previous production version without engineer review, to save time
Disable all logging and monitoring temporarily so the elevated error rate does not affect dashboards during investigation
Grant Claude Code full write access to the production database so it can directly repair any corrupted records it identifies

Provide Claude Code with read access to recent logs, error traces, and the relevant service code so it can help correlate the error pattern with a recent change, while the engineer reviews and validates any proposed fix before deployment
correct_answer: Provide Claude Code with read access to recent logs, error traces, and the relevant service code so it can help correlate the error pattern with a recent change, while the engineer reviews and validates any proposed fix before deployment
explanation: Supporting debugging and operational issue resolution effectively means using AI tooling to accelerate diagnosis (correlating logs, traces, and code changes, option D) while keeping a human in the loop for validation and deployment decisions, especially during a live incident. Allowing autonomous production rollbacks (A) or direct database writes (C) without human review introduces unacceptable operational risk. Disabling monitoring (B) removes the very telemetry needed to diagnose and resolve the issue.

text: A team lead notices that engineers frequently ask Claude Code to re-explain the same internal API conventions, build commands, and deployment steps in every new session, wasting tokens and time. Which configuration change would most directly improve developer productivity for this recurring pattern?
options: Instruct engineers to retype the full explanation from memory each time to reinforce learning

Create a persistent project-level instructions file (e.g., a `CLAUDE.md`-style context file) documenting conventions, build commands, and deployment steps so this context is automatically available in every session
Increase the model's temperature setting so it infers conventions more creatively without needing documentation
Switch to a smaller model that responds faster regardless of whether it has the necessary context
correct_answer: Create a persistent project-level instructions file (e.g., a `CLAUDE.md`-style context file) documenting conventions, build commands, and deployment steps so this context is automatically available in every session
explanation: A core operational enablement practice is configuring team environments so recurring context (conventions, build/deploy commands) is persisted and automatically loaded (B), avoiding repeated manual re-explanation across sessions. This reduces wasted tokens and engineer time. Manually retyping (A) wastes effort. Raising temperature (C) affects output randomness, not context availability, and could reduce consistency. Switching to a smaller model (D) does not solve the underlying missing-context problem and may degrade quality.

text: A team has integrated Claude into their CI/CD pipeline to auto-generate unit tests for new pull requests. Over several weeks, engineers notice that generated tests often pass trivially (e.g., asserting true) rather than meaningfully exercising edge cases, and this is not caught until manual review later in the sprint. What is the best operational enablement fix to catch this issue earlier in the developer workflow?
options: Add an automated check in the pipeline that measures code coverage and flags trivial or low-assertion-density tests for mandatory human review before merge, rather than relying solely on later manual review
Remove automated test generation entirely since it cannot be trusted
Increase the number of tests Claude generates per PR without changing how they are evaluated
Allow PRs to merge automatically whenever any tests are present, regardless of their quality
correct_answer: Add an automated check in the pipeline that measures code coverage and flags trivial or low-assertion-density tests for mandatory human review before merge, rather than relying solely on later manual review
explanation: Effective operational enablement means closing the feedback loop early in the workflow rather than discovering quality issues late. Adding automated coverage/assertion-density checks (A) surfaces low-quality generated tests at PR time, prompting review before merge. Removing generation (B) discards the productivity benefit without addressing the root cause. Generating more tests without better evaluation (C) compounds the problem. Auto-merging based on test presence alone (D) ignores quality entirely and increases risk of undetected defects reaching production.
